vectors.description: The same defect shape as contributionPreference: neither engine validated it, so an unrecognized method silently fell through to the default employer formula.

vectors.name: 1989 fractional plan-term capacity keeps its fraction in the message
vectors.description: 1989 IRC 415(c)(1)(B) allowed 25 percent of compensation, so 25 percent of 100018 is 25004.50, less the 1989 IRC 402(g) elective-deferral limit of 7627, leaving 17377.50 of capacity that depends on unstated plan terms. The message must print 17,377.5, not a rounded 17,378; PHP rendered money to two decimals where the TypeScript default carries three.

expect.accounts.0.diagnostics.0.message: $17,377.5 of potential annual-additions capacity requires an employer contribution formula or permission for voluntary after-tax contributions.

vectors.name: flag field that is not a boolean is rejected
vectors.description: The string "0" is truthy in JavaScript and falsy in PHP, so coercing it made a 1980 traditional IRA ineligible in one engine and determinate in the other from the same input. Flag fields must be actual booleans; an empty array is the same trap.

vectors.name: 2026 unmarried qualified HSA funding distribution reduces the limit under IRC 223(b)(4)(C)
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection" by the sum of its subparagraphs, of which "(C) the aggregate amount contributed to health savings accounts of such individual for such taxable year under section 408(d)(9)". Twelve self-only months give 12 x (4400/12) = 4400 under IRC 223(b)(2)(A) with the 2026 amount from Rev. Proc. 2025-19; the $1,500 rolled over from an IRA under IRC 408(d)(9) reduces it to 4400 - 1500 = 2900.

vectors.name: 2026 qualified HSA funding distribution reaches the IRC 223(b)(3) additional contribution amount
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation applying "under this subsection", which for an individual who attained 55 before the close of the year is the IRC 223(b)(1) limitation as increased by IRC 223(b)(3). Twelve self-only months in 2026 give 4400 and the IRC 223(b)(3)(B) table gives 1000 for 2009 and thereafter, so subsection (b) allows 5400; a $5,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution reduces it to 400. The subsection is reduced once as a whole, so paragraph (1) absorbs 4400 and only the 600 it could not absorb reaches the 1000, leaving 400. hsa.additionalContributionAmount reports the unreduced statutory 1000.

vectors.name: 2026 IRC 223(b)(4) reduces by the sum of subparagraphs (A) and (C) but not below zero
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(4) reduces the limitation "(but not below zero) by the sum of" its subparagraphs, so 1200 paid to Archer MSAs and 3400 contributed under IRC 408(d)(9) reduce the 2026 twelve-month self-only limitation of 4400 by 4600 and leave 0 rather than -200. The fall is attributed in subparagraph order: (A) takes the first 1200 in full, leaving 3200, and (C) can only reach that 3200 of the remaining ceiling even though 3400 was contributed.

vectors.name: 2026 married qualified HSA funding distribution is taken after the IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) division
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(4) flush text says "Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any individual to whom paragraph (5) applies" and names subparagraph (A) alone, so subparagraph (C) survives for a married individual; and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) reduces the family limitation only "by the aggregate amount paid to Archer MSAs of such spouses", so nothing routes (C) through paragraph (5). It is an amount of "such individual", so it reduces that spouse's own subsection (b) limitation after the division. The 2026 family limitation of 8750 divides equally to 4375 each; the taxpayer's $2,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution leaves the taxpayer 2375 and the spouse untouched at 4375. Taken before the division like the Archer reduction it would have given (8750 - 2000) / 2 = 3375 to each and charged the spouse for the taxpayer's rollover.

vectors.name: 2026 matched Archer MSA contribution of the same amount is taken before the division instead
vectors.description: The same couple and the same $2,000, paid to Archer MSAs instead of contributed under IRC 408(d)(9), goes through IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) and reduces the single family limitation before (ii) divides it: 8750 - 2000 = 6750 divided equally is 3375 each. Pairing this with the IRC 408(d)(9) vector isolates the ordering rather than the amount — 2375/4375 under subparagraph (C) against 3375/3375 under IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) — which is what the flush text naming only subparagraph (A) produces.

vectors.name: 2026 married qualified HSA funding distribution reaches that spouse's IRC 223(b)(3) amount
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B) reduces and divides the paragraph (1) limitation "without regard to any additional contribution amount under paragraph (3)", so the Archer reduction can never reach a married individual's age-55 amount. Subparagraph (C) is not part of paragraph (5): it reduces the limitation applying to the individual "under this subsection", which after the division is that spouse's 4375 share plus their own 1000, so it does reach it. A $5,000 IRC 408(d)(9) contribution by a taxpayer aged 55 or over takes the 4375 to 0 and the remaining 625 off the 1000, leaving 375; the spouse keeps 4375 + 1000 = 5375.

vectors.name: 2026 qualified HSA funding distribution follows the IRC 223(b)(8) last-month rule on both sides
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(8)(A) applies "for purposes of computing the limitation under paragraph (1)" and IRC 223(b)(4) reduces "the limitation which would (but for this paragraph) apply under this subsection", so the reduction follows the last-month rule. December-only self-only coverage with the election gives 4400, less the $200 contributed under IRC 408(d)(9) is 4200. The counterfactual month-by-month limitation is 4400/12 = 366.67, and the same 200 reduces it to 166.67, so the amount that "could not have been made but for" IRC 223(b)(8)(A) under IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i)(I) is 4200 - 166.67 = 4033.33. Measuring it against the unreduced 366.67 counterfactual would understate it by the 200 that never applied. hsa.contributionLimitWithoutLastMonthRule reports the unreduced 366.67.

vectors.name: 2026 family-limit shares totalling exactly one may still give a spouse nothing
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) constrains the division, not either share within it, so an agreement of 1 and 0 divides the whole 2026 family limitation of 8750 to one spouse and leaves the other 0. The shares total exactly 1, so the division is complete and the result stays determinate: the guard is on the sum, not on any share being positive.

vectors.name: 2026 sole HSA-owning spouse may agree a share below one without forfeiting anything
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides the limitation between the spouses, and the shares that can be supplied cover only spouses who own a health savings account. Where one spouse owns none, a share of 0.6 on the other is a complete division whose remaining 0.4 the first spouse has no account to use, not an under-allocation, so no shares-below-one error applies: 0.6 x 8750 = 5250. Pinning the first diagnostic as the general disclaimer proves neither HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_SHARES_BELOW_ONE nor the equal-division default fired.

vectors.name: 2026 flexible spending arrangement parameters are published in the result
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 sets the 2026 IRC 125(i) dollar limitation on health FSA salary reduction contributions at 3400 and states that where the cafeteria plan permits a carryover the maximum carryover amount is 680, which is 20 percent of 3400 under Notice 2020-33. Pub. L. 119-21 section 70404 struck "$5,000 ($2,500" from IRC 129(a)(2)(A) and inserted "$7,500 ($3,750" for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, so the 2026 dependent care exclusion is 7500 and 3750 on a married separate return. The scenario result carries these alongside hsaParameters whether or not the scenario holds any flexible spending arrangement.

vectors.name: 2012 health FSA exists with no statutory ceiling rather than not existing
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) reaches plan years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling. The arrangement existed, though, so the row records the state rather than being absent: an absent row means the program did not exist, which is a different fact and produces a different result.

vectors.name: 1986 has an IRC 129 row with no dollar ceiling; 1981 has no row at all
vectors.description: Pub. L. 97-34 section 124 added IRC 129 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981, and Pub. L. 99-514 section 1163(a) added its dollar limitation for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986. 1986 therefore sits in the middle state: the exclusion existed with no statutory ceiling, which the table records rather than omits. The unavailable years are the ones with no row, which is what makes the table minimum the statement of when IRC 129 began.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA election at the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 sets the 2026 dollar limitation under IRC 125(i) on voluntary employee salary reductions for contributions to health flexible spending arrangements at 3400, so an employee electing the maximum elects 3400. IRC 125(a) keeps the salary reduction out of gross income, so the whole 3400 comes out of Form W-2 box 1 and out of social security and medicare wages under IRC 3121(a)(5)(G) and none of it appears in federalAgiReduction, which reports above-the-line deductions.

vectors.name: 2013 is the first year IRC 125(i) limits a health FSA election
vectors.description: IRC 125(i)(1) fixes the limit at 2500 and IRC 125(i)(2) begins indexing only for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2013, so 2013 carries the raw statutory amount. No annual revenue procedure states it: Rev. Proc. 2012-41's list of 2013 adjusted items has no Cafeteria Plans entry, and Notice 2012-40 is the operative authority. Paired with the 2012 vector, this pins the effective date rather than the figure alone.

vectors.name: 2012 health FSA has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) was added by Pub. L. 111-148 section 9005 and Notice 2012-40 section II records that before its effective date plan sponsors imposed their own limits but there was no statutory limit. Notice 2012-40 section III reads the effective date as reaching plan years beginning after December 31, 2012. A health FSA therefore existed in 2012 and could receive salary reductions; what did not exist is a ceiling. The result is indeterminate with a null statutory maximum rather than unavailable with a zero, which is what the account type not existing would produce, and rather than a 2500 borrowed from the following year.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA carryover is capped by the 2025 cap and the excess is forfeited
vectors.description: Notice 2020-33 section III.A sets the carryover at 20 percent of the IRC 125(i) limit for the plan year the amounts are carried FROM, and Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.16 states 660 for a plan year beginning in 2025, which is 20 percent of that year's 3300 limit. Notice 2013-71 section III makes the carried amount the lesser of the unused amount and the cap, and forfeits the rest: 900 unused gives 660 carried and 240 forfeited. The receiving year's cap of 680 is a different figure and does not govern this carryover, which is the error a receiving-year reading would make.

vectors.name: 2026 health FSA carryover sits on top of the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section III holds that in addition to the carried-over amount the plan may permit the individual to elect up to the maximum allowed salary reduction, so the carryover "does not count against or otherwise affect" the IRC 125(i) limit. A 400 carryover out of the 2025 plan year, below that year's 660 cap so nothing is forfeited, therefore leaves the 2026 ceiling at the full 3400 from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15, and 3800 is available to pay claims incurred in 2026. Implementing the carryover as a reduction would give 3000 here, which is why this needs its own vector.

vectors.name: a health FSA grace period precludes a carryover
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV holds that a plan providing for a carryover may not also provide a grace period, and conversely a plan that offers the Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-1(e) grace period carries nothing over. Nothing is carried in, and no forfeiture figure is produced because how much of the prior year's balance survives depends on expenses incurred during the two-month-and-15-day grace period, which is not a tax parameter. Paired with the carryover vector on the same 900 unused amount, this shows the plan option and not the amount is what decides.

vectors.name: a health FSA offering neither carryover nor grace period forfeits the whole unused amount
vectors.description: Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-5(c) requires unused benefits or contributions remaining at the end of the plan year to be forfeited, which Notice 2013-71 calls the use-or-lose rule. A plan that offers no carryover forfeits all 900, not the 240 excess above the 660 cap that a carryover plan would forfeit. The forfeiture is reported rather than silently dropped.

vectors.name: a health FSA carryover and grace period asserted together are refused
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV: a section 125 cafeteria plan that incorporates a carryover provision may not also provide for a grace period in the plan year to which unused amounts may be carried over. Asserting both describes a plan that cannot exist, so a determinate carryover figure computed from either fact would assert something the guidance forbids. The result is indeterminate with no statutory maximum and no carryover cap, following the treatment of shares that do not divide the IRC 223(b)(5) family limitation.

vectors.name: nothing may be carried into 2013, the first year the carryover existed
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section IV permits a plan to adopt the carryover for a plan year beginning in 2013, so 2013 is the first plan year amounts may be carried FROM and 2014 the first year they may land in. There is consequently no 2012 cap, and a 2013 scenario asserting a carryover of a prior-year unused amount cannot be answered: the cap that governs belongs to the source year. Reporting zero carried would be indistinguishable from a plan that forfeited, so the result is indeterminate.

vectors.name: a 2021 health FSA carryover out of 2020 discloses that CAA 2021 section 214 relief is not modelled
vectors.description: Rev. Proc. 2019-44 section 3.17 sets the 2020 IRC 125(i) limit at 2750 and Notice 2020-33 section III.A states 550 as the maximum unused amount from a plan year starting in 2020, being 20 percent of 2750. Section 214 of Pub. L. 116-260, implemented by Notice 2021-15 section III.A, separately permitted a plan to carry over ALL unused amounts from a plan year ending in 2020 to the plan year ending in 2021. Adopting that was entirely a plan option, so the ordinary cap is applied and the divergence is disclosed rather than left silent: 900 unused gives 550 carried under the ordinary cap and would give 900 under section 214 relief.

vectors.name: a prior-year unused amount without a stated plan option asks for the fact
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 makes the carryover and the grace period plan options that a plan may adopt, may adopt one of, or may adopt neither, and they are mutually exclusive. An unused amount alone therefore does not determine what happens to it. Assuming a carryover would report 660 carried and assuming forfeiture would report 900 forfeited, so the engine reports neither, asks for the fact, and marks the result determinate with assumptions.

vectors.name: a health FSA election above the IRC 125(i) limit is reported, not truncated
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) makes a health FSA a qualified benefit only if the plan provides that an employee may not elect salary reduction contributions above the limit, and Notice 2012-40 section III holds that a plan failing to comply is not a section 125 cafeteria plan at all, so the value of the taxable benefits the employee could have elected is includible regardless of the benefit elected. A 4000 election for 2026 against the 3400 limit from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 is therefore an error carrying a plan-qualification consequence, and truncating it to 3400 would report a smaller consequence than the statute produces. The 600 excess is reported and nothing further is allocated. Notice 2012-40 section III costs the plan its IRC 125 status entirely rather than only as to the excess, so the IRC 125(a) exclusion fails for the whole 4000: the election stays in contributionComponents as a fact, and no wage exclusion is reported for it.

vectors.name: an account type that did not exist for the tax year reports no exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 223 was added by the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 section 1201 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2003, so there is no health savings account for 2003. A cafeteria-plan contribution supplied against one is still recorded, because the scenario said it happened, but it cannot carry the IRC 106(d) exclusion of an account type that did not exist: no reduction of Form W-2 box 1 wages and none of social security and medicare wages is reported.

vectors.name: a pre-2013 health FSA still excludes its salary reduction under IRC 125(a)
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) was added by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act section 9005 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary reduction ceiling to report and the account is indeterminate. The arrangement existed, though, and IRC 125(a) excluded its salary reduction from gross income exactly as it does now. An indeterminate limit is not a reason to withhold the exclusion: the 3000 elected is outside Form W-2 box 1 and outside social security and medicare wages. This is the deliberate contrast with an unavailable account type and with an IRC 125(i) qualification failure, where the exclusion genuinely does not apply.

vectors.name: a pre-2013 health FSA with a supplied plan maximum reports that maximum
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) reaches plan years beginning after December 31, 2012, so 2012 has no statutory salary-reduction ceiling. The arrangement existed and the ceiling was whatever the plan document imposed. Where the caller supplies that document, the maximum is knowable and is reported: the statutory maximum stays null because no statute set one, while the maximum the inputs support is the plan's own 2000. Refusing to answer here would discard a fact the caller gave, and a diagnostic records that the figure rests on the plan term alone.

vectors.name: two unrelated employers each carry a full health FSA limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: an employee employed by two or more employers that are not members of the same controlled group may elect up to the indexed limit under each employer's health FSA. For 2026 that is 3400 under each of two unrelated employers and 6800 in total, which is the answer a single per-person limit would get wrong.

vectors.name: two health FSAs of one employer share a single IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: all employers treated as a single employer under IRC 414(b), (c) or (m) are treated as one for the limit, and an employee participating in multiple cafeteria plans of that group is limited to the indexed amount in total under IRC 125(g)(4). Two arrangements carrying the same employerId therefore draw on one 3400 pool for 2026, not two, so the first exhausts it and the second has nothing left. Paired with the two-unrelated-employers vector, this pins that employerId is what separates the limits.

vectors.name: spouses filing jointly each carry a full health FSA limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: the limit applies on an employee-by-employee basis, so if each of two spouses is eligible to elect salary reduction contributions each may elect up to the indexed amount, even in the same health FSA sponsored by the same employer. For 2026 that is 3400 each and 6800 in total. This is the deliberate contrast with IRC 129(a)(2)(A), which is a per-return household amount.

vectors.name: non-elective employer flex credits stay outside the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: the limit applies only to salary reduction contributions and not to employer non-elective contributions, sometimes called flex credits, and its worked example is an employer contributing a 500 flex credit to each employee's health FSA for the plan year, after which each employee may still elect the full indexed amount. For 2026 the employee therefore still elects 3400 alongside a 500 non-elective credit.

vectors.name: flex credits electable as cash consume the IRC 125(i) limit
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III: if an employer provides flex credits that employees may elect to receive as cash or as a taxable benefit, those flex credits are treated as salary reduction contributions for purposes of IRC 125(i). A 500 cashable credit against the 3400 limit from Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 therefore leaves 2900 of election room. Paired with the non-elective vector at the same 500, this pins that the cash election and not the credit is what matters.

vectors.name: flex credits without a stated cash election ask for the fact
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 makes the answer turn entirely on whether the employee could have elected the credit as cash or another taxable benefit, and that is a plan-design fact this engine cannot read. The ordinary case under Prop. Treas. Reg. 1.125-5(b) is a non-elective credit, so the full 3400 is reported, but the assumption is stated rather than silent and the status records it.

vectors.name: a lower plan-document health FSA limit binds
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 section III records that a plan may specify a lower amount than the statutory maximum, and Notice 2012-40 section II notes that before IRC 125(i) plan sponsors imposed their own limits. A plan capping elections at 2000 for 2026 therefore binds below the 3400 statutory ceiling. The two are reported separately rather than merged: statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution is what IRC 125(i) sets, and maximumAnnualContributionBasedOnInputs is what the supplied plan document allows within it. Reporting 2000 as the statutory maximum would attribute the plan sponsor's own term to the statute.

vectors.name: a lower plan-document limit caps its own arrangement, not the employer group
vectors.description: IRC 125(g)(4) treats employers under IRC 414(b), (c) or (m) as one employer, which Notice 2012-40 applies to aggregate elections across their cafeteria plans against the one statutory ceiling. It aggregates to the statutory amount; it does not turn one plan's own lower term into an employer-wide ceiling. A plan document capping elections at 2000 binds elections under that plan and gives it no power over a different plan of the same group, so for 2026 the first arrangement reaches 2000, the second reaches the 1400 left of the shared 3400, and the group total is 3400 rather than 2000.

vectors.name: exceeding a plan-document limit is not the IRC 125(i) qualification failure
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III holds that a cafeteria plan permitting an election above the IRC 125(i) limit is not an IRC 125 cafeteria plan at all, which is why an election above the statutory ceiling reports no IRC 125(a) exclusion. That holding addresses the statutory limit. An election of 3000 against a plan document allowing 2000 stays within the 3400 IRC 125(i) ceiling for 2026, so it is a plan-operation question rather than a statutory qualification failure: it is reported, but the exclusion is not withdrawn, and the 3000 remains outside Form W-2 box 1 and outside social security and medicare wages.

vectors.name: a non-calendar cafeteria plan year makes the IRC 125(i) figure indeterminate
vectors.description: Notice 2012-40 section III holds that "taxable year" in IRC 125(i) refers to the plan year of the cafeteria plan, so the limit runs on a plan-year basis and a short plan year is prorated by its months, while every annual revenue procedure publishes the figure for taxable years beginning in a calendar year and this package is keyed by tax year. The two agree exactly for a calendar-year plan. For any other plan year the governing figure depends on the plan year start date, which is not an input, so the result is indeterminate rather than the calendar-year figure assumed.

vectors.name: a bare FSA account type is rejected as ambiguous
vectors.description: Input-contract assertion rather than a computed amount. "FSA" names an IRC 125(i) health flexible spending arrangement and an IRC 129 dependent care assistance program equally well, and the two carry different limits, different authorities, and different household aggregation - IRC 125(i) is per employee per employer while IRC 129(a)(2)(A) is per return. Aliasing the bare string would silently pick one of them, so it is rejected and the message names both spellings.

vectors.name: an unrecognised health FSA purpose is rejected
vectors.description: Input-contract assertion rather than a computed amount. Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifies a health FSA as general-purpose, limited-purpose, or post-deductible, and the three lead to different IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) answers. A fourth spelling is not a fourth classification, so it is rejected rather than treated as unstated, which would silently downgrade a stated fact into the diagnose-and-ask path.

vectors.name: 2025 dependent care assistance exclusion on a single return
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) sets the amount excludable for dependent care services provided during a taxable year at 5000, and the amount is not inflation adjusted, so no revenue procedure states it and 2025 carries the same figure the Tax Reform Act of 1986 put there. IRC 129(a)(1) excludes it from gross income, so it comes out of Form W-2 box 1 and out of social security and medicare wages under IRC 3121(a)(18) and contributes nothing to federalAgiReduction. The employee's 60000 of earned income does not bind under IRC 129(b)(1)(A).

vectors.name: 2025 dependent care exclusion is halved on a married separate return
vectors.description: The IRC 129(a)(2)(A) parenthetical sets the amount at 2500 in the case of a separate return by a married individual. Married separate spouses file separate returns, so each carries their own 2500 rather than dividing one 5000, which is why the amount is halved rather than shared. IRC 129(b)(1)(B) needs both spouses' earned income; 60000 and 55000 leave the statutory amount binding. IRC 129(a)(2)(C) takes marital status from IRC 21(e)(3) and (4) rather than from the filing status alone, and the IRC 21(e)(4) facts are not derivable from anything supplied, so the halved amount is applied and the undetermined status is reported rather than assumed away.

vectors.name: an IRC 21(e)(4) considered-unmarried separate return takes the undivided amount
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(C) determines marital status under IRC 21(e)(3) and (4). IRC 21(e)(4) treats a married individual filing separately as not married when they maintained a household that was a qualifying individual's principal place of abode for more than half the taxable year, furnished over half the cost of maintaining it, and their spouse was not a member of it during the last six months. Such a taxpayer is not married for IRC 129, so for 2026 they take the undivided 7500 rather than the halved 3750, and the IRC 129(b)(1)(A) limitation is their own 90000 earned income rather than the IRC 129(b)(1)(B) lesser of the two spouses' 3000. Both halves of the rule move together: applying one without the other reproduces neither the married nor the unmarried treatment.

vectors.name: a separate return that states it is still married keeps the halved amount
vectors.description: The contrast with the vector above. Stating treatedAsUnmarriedUnderSection21e4 as false is the IRC 21(e)(4) determination made and answered in the negative, so the halved 3750 and the IRC 129(b)(1)(B) lesser-of rule apply exactly as they do without the fact -- but the result is determinate rather than carrying the undetermined-status warning, because the caller has answered the question.

vectors.name: 2021 only, the ARPA dependent care exclusion is 10500
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(D), added by the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, Pub. L. 117-2 section 9632(a), applies subparagraph (A) for a taxable year beginning after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2022 by substituting "$10,500 (half such dollar amount" for "$5,000 ($2,500". The statute writes the separate-return amount as half rather than as a number, and half of 10500 is 5250. Enacted in March 2021, so Rev. Proc. 2020-45 could not carry it; the authority is the act.

vectors.name: 2022 reverts to the pre-ARPA dependent care exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(D) reaches only a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2022, so the substitution lapses and subparagraph (A) applies unmodified from 2022: 5000, or 2500 on a married separate return. A 2021-only vector passes even if the reversion is missing entirely, which is why the pair is needed rather than the single year.

vectors.name: 2026 dependent care exclusion rises to 7500 under Pub. L. 119-21
vectors.description: Pub. L. 119-21 section 70404(a) amends IRC 129(a)(2)(A) by striking "$5,000 ($2,500" and inserting "$7,500 ($3,750", and section 70404(b) applies the amendment to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. It is a fixed-dollar substitution that adds no indexing mechanism. Paired with the 2025 vector this pins the effective date; the 2024 edition of the Code still prints the old figures, so a year block generated from the Code text alone would be wrong here.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) earned income limitation binds below the statutory amount
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1)(B) caps the amount excluded at the lesser of the employee's and the spouse's earned income for the taxable year. A spouse with 3000 of earned income against the employee's 90000 therefore caps the exclusion at 3000, well below the 7500 that IRC 129(a)(2)(A) allows for 2026. Both figures are caller-supplied, which is what keeps this inside a package that does not derive income. The two ceilings are reported separately: statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution is the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount and maximumAnnualContributionBasedOnInputs is what the supplied earned income allows within it.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) limitation is asked for when the earned income facts are absent
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1)(B) caps the exclusion at the lesser of the employee's and the spouse's earned income, and on a joint return both are needed. Only the employee's is supplied here. The ceiling is mandatory rather than an optional refinement, so reporting the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount as what the inputs support would assume the missing spouse's earned income is at least 7500 -- an assumption the statute never permits. The result fails closed: the statutory amount is still reported, the amount the inputs support is null, and the diagnostic names the missing fact.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(2) deemed earned income schedule is disclosed as unmodelled
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(2) applies IRC 21(d)(2) to deem earned income for a spouse who is a student or incapable of caring for himself. The IRC 21(d)(2) monthly schedule is a figure this package does not encode, because no primary source for it is committed to the evidence corpus and an unattested amount is never encoded. The supplied spouse figure of 500 is therefore used exactly as stated - as the deemed amount - and the divergence is disclosed rather than silently filled in. Both earned income figures are supplied, so the result stays determinate with assumptions rather than failing closed; what is disclosed is that the supplied 500 is used exactly as stated rather than derived from the IRC 21(d)(2) schedule.

vectors.name: spouses filing jointly share one IRC 129 household exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) limits the amount which may be excluded for dependent care services provided during a taxable year, and IRC 129(a)(2)(C) determines marital status under IRC 21(e)(3) and (4); it is a per-return figure, not a per-person one. Two spouses electing 5000 each for 2026 against the 7500 household amount therefore exclude 7500 in total, not 15000, and IRC 129(a)(2)(B) includes the remaining 2500 in gross income for the taxable year the services were provided. This is the deliberate contrast with IRC 125(i), which is per employee and gives each spouse a full limit.

vectors.name: married separate spouses do not share one IRC 129 exclusion
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) is per return and married separate spouses file two returns, so each carries their own halved 3750 amount for 2026 rather than dividing a single 7500. Two 3750 elections are therefore both wholly excludable and nothing is includible, which pooling them would get wrong by including 3750. Paired with the joint vector on the same two elections, this pins that filing status and not marriage decides the pooling.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling is a return-level figure across two dependent care FSAs
vectors.description: IRC 129(b)(1) caps "the amount excluded from the income of an employee under subsection (a) for any taxable year", which is that year's aggregate rather than a per-plan figure, and Form 2441 Part III computes one excluded-benefits amount for the return as the smallest of the benefits received, the employee's earned income, the spouse's earned income, and the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount. A spouse earning 3000 therefore caps the whole return at 3000, not at 3000 for each dependent care FSA it holds: of the 10000 elected across two arrangements, 3000 is excluded and IRC 129(a)(2)(B) includes the remaining 7000 in gross income. Applied per account the same facts would exclude 6000.

vectors.name: a dependent care plan document below the IRC 129 amount binds this arrangement
vectors.description: Form 2441's dependent care benefit computation takes the maximum permitted under the employer's plan into account when it is below the Code amount. A plan allowing 4000 for 2026 therefore binds below the 7500 IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount, and the statutory figure is still reported separately so the source of the constraint is visible rather than merged into one number.

vectors.name: a dependent care plan document caps its own arrangement, not the household amount
vectors.description: The IRC 129(a)(2)(A) amount is the return's and a plan document is one plan's own term, so the two constrain different things. For 2026 an arrangement allowing 2000 reaches 2000, and a second arrangement with no such term still reaches the remaining 5500 of the 7500 household amount. A plan document that lowered the household figure would forfeit 5500 of capacity the Code allows.

vectors.name: the IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling does not pool across married separate returns
vectors.description: IRC 129(a)(2)(A) gives a married individual filing separately half the amount, and the two spouses file two returns rather than one, so each draws on its own 3750 for 2026. The IRC 129(b)(1) ceiling follows the same scope: it caps the exclusion on each return, so a lesser earned income of 3000 binds each return at 3000 rather than binding 3000 across both. Each spouse electing 3500 therefore excludes 3000 and includes 500, and the pair excludes 6000 in total. This is the deliberate contrast with the joint-return vector above, where one ceiling covers both arrangements.

vectors.name: 1986 dependent care has no statutory ceiling, so the earned income limitation is the ceiling
vectors.description: Pub. L. 99-514 section 1163(a) added the IRC 129(a)(2)(A) dollar limitation for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, so 1986 has none. IRC 129 existed and excluded the assistance, and IRC 129(b)(1) still capped it at the employee's earned income. With 40000 of earned income supplied that is the only ceiling there was, and it is a real answer: the statutory maximum is null while the maximum the inputs support is 40000. Reporting nothing here would discard a fact the caller gave.

vectors.name: 1986 dependent care with no ceiling from any source stays indeterminate
vectors.description: The contrast with the vector above. Without a statutory ceiling, and with neither the IRC 129(b)(1) earned income facts nor a plan maximum supplied, there is no ceiling from any source and no maximum is reported. The absence of a statutory figure is not by itself a reason to refuse; the absence of every figure is.

vectors.name: 1981 predates IRC 129 entirely
vectors.description: The effective-date note to IRC 129 makes the section applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981, under section 124(f) of the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, Pub. L. 97-34. For 1981 there was no dependent care assistance exclusion at all, which is a different fact from the 1982 through 1986 years where the exclusion existed without a ceiling. The two therefore report differently: unavailable with a zero here, indeterminate with a null there.

vectors.name: a health FSA and a dependent care FSA carry independent limits
vectors.description: IRC 125(i) limits salary reduction contributions to a health flexible spending arrangement and Notice 2012-40 section III states expressly that it does not limit employee salary reduction contributions to an FSA for dependent care assistance, which IRC 129(a)(2)(A) governs separately. For 2026 an employee may therefore elect 3400 under Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.15 and 7500 under IRC 129(a)(2)(A) as amended by Pub. L. 119-21 section 70404, and the two figures never draw on one another.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA is diagnosed against an HSA without changing the IRC 223 figures
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 1 holds that an individual covered by an HDHP and by a health FSA paying or reimbursing section 213(d) medical expenses before the IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) minimum annual deductible is satisfied is not an eligible individual, because IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) requires that an eligible individual not be covered by a plan that is not an HDHP and that provides coverage for a benefit the HDHP covers. The conflict is reported and not enforced: eligible-individual status is a caller-supplied fact everywhere in this engine and no rule overrides one, so the caller who has already accounted for it still gets the answer their months imply. Rev. Proc. 2025-19 sets the 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(A) self-only limitation at 4400, and that figure and the amount the inputs support must both survive untouched - asserting them is the whole point, since a rule that zeroed or reduced the limit would still pass a vector that only checked the diagnostic.

vectors.name: a limited-purpose health FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 2 holds that where the medical expenses paid or reimbursed include only vision and dental benefits, which are permitted coverage, and preventive care, the individual is an eligible individual. No conflict diagnostic is emitted and the account stays determinate, which is what separates this from the general-purpose case on otherwise identical inputs.

vectors.name: a post-deductible health FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 Situation 4 holds that where the health FSA pays or reimburses medical expenses only after the HDHP's minimum annual deductible has been satisfied, including coinsurance the HDHP does not cover, the individual is an eligible individual. The third of the three Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifications, encoded because it produces the opposite answer from the first on the same account type.

vectors.name: a health FSA of unstated purpose makes the IRC 223 limitation indeterminate
vectors.description: The three Rev. Rul. 2004-45 classifications give two opposite IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) answers, and which applies is a plan-design fact this engine cannot read. Unlike the general-purpose case, where the conflict is known and the caller's own figures are returned, here nothing about IRC 223 is known, so a confident 4400 would be the defect rather than the diagnostic. The limitation is refused and the purpose is asked for. The health FSA's own disqualifiesHsaEligibility is null for the same reason.

vectors.name: a spouse's general-purpose health FSA disqualifies the other spouse's HSA
vectors.description: Rev. Rul. 2004-45 states expressly, after the Situation 1 holding, that the result is the same if the individual is covered by a health FSA sponsored by the employer of the individual's spouse, because such an arrangement can reimburse this individual's own section 213(d) medical expenses. The conflict is household-level, not per-person. The diagnostic lands on the HSA owner's account even though the arrangement belongs to the other spouse, and the IRC 223(b) figures are unchanged for the same reason they are in the individual case. The spouse's empty persons[].hsaCoverage records that they held no HDHP coverage, which is what IRC 223(b)(5)(A) needs to know.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA carryover disqualifies the whole receiving plan year
vectors.description: Notice 2013-71 makes the carried-over amount available to pay medical expenses incurred during the entire plan year to which it is carried. Carried-over general-purpose funds are therefore general-purpose coverage for that whole year, not just until they are spent, so the Rev. Rul. 2004-45 disqualification reaches the receiving year rather than a part of it. Rev. Proc. 2024-40 section 3.16 caps the carryover out of 2025 at 660, and the diagnostic says so; the IRC 223 figures are unchanged as in every other branch of this interaction.

vectors.name: a general-purpose health FSA grace period extends the IRC 223 disqualification
vectors.description: Notice 2005-86 holds that an individual participating in a health FSA who is covered by the grace period is generally not eligible to contribute to an HSA until the first day of the first month following the end of that grace period, even where the participant's health FSA has no unused benefits at the end of the prior plan year. The grace-period months fall in the following plan year, which this year's eligible-month input cannot express, so the extension is reported as information alongside the disqualification rather than folded into the month list.

vectors.name: a dependent care FSA raises no IRC 223 conflict at all
vectors.description: IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) reaches coverage providing a benefit the high deductible health plan covers, and an IRC 129 dependent care assistance program reimburses dependent care expenses rather than section 213(d) medical expenses, so Rev. Rul. 2004-45 has nothing to say about it. A dependent care FSA alongside an HSA is therefore an ordinary determinate scenario, which is worth pinning because the two account types were added together and a purpose check written against the wrong family would fire here.

vectors.name: 2026 defined benefit plan reports the IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 states that effective January 1, 2026 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under section 415(b)(1)(A) of the Code is increased from $280,000 to $290,000", so the 2026 annual benefit limit is $290,000; the figure is transcribed from that notice in evidence/retirement-limits and its document is fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt. That limitation caps the benefit the plan may pay and is not a contribution ceiling: sizing a defined-benefit contribution runs through IRC 404, IRC 412 and the ERISA funding rules from the plan formula, participant census, assets and actuarial assumptions, none of which this package models. The account therefore keeps a null statutory maximum, an indeterminate status and DEFINED_BENEFIT_CONTRIBUTION_REQUIRES_ACTUARIAL_VALUATION, and reports the benefit limit beside them. Pinning both halves is the point: the benefit ceiling is knowable from the tax year alone, the contribution is not, and neither answer may be derived from the other.

vectors.name: 2011 cash balance plan reports the transcribed IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: A cash balance plan is a defined benefit plan that states the benefit as a hypothetical account balance, so IRC 415(b) governs it and IRC 415(c) does not; it takes the same treatment here as a traditional pension. Notice 2010-78 states that effective January 1, 2011 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under 415(b)(1)(A) remains unchanged at $195,000". "Remains unchanged" is the notice publishing the figure for 2011, not declining to: an amount the IRS restates for a year is transcribed for that year like any other, and 195000 is recorded for 2011 in evidence/retirement-limits from the document fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt. It is not carried forward from the 195000 recorded for 2010, which SOURCES.md would forbid. The account still keeps a null statutory maximum and an indeterminate status, because IRC 415(b)(1)(A) caps the benefit the plan may pay and says nothing about the contribution needed to fund it; the actuarial-valuation diagnostic is therefore still the first diagnostic on the account, with the benefit-limit report beside it.

vectors.name: 2012 cash balance plan reports the transcribed IRC 415(b)(1)(A) annual benefit limit
vectors.description: A cash balance plan is a defined benefit plan that states the benefit as a hypothetical account balance, so IRC 415(b) governs it and IRC 415(c) does not; it takes the same treatment here as a traditional pension. Notice 2011-90 states that effective January 1, 2012 "the limitation on the annual benefit under a defined benefit plan under 415(b)(1)(A) is increased from $195,000 to $200,000". The account still keeps a null statutory maximum and an indeterminate status, because IRC 415(b)(1)(A) caps the benefit the plan may pay and says nothing about the contribution needed to fund it; the actuarial-valuation diagnostic is therefore still the first diagnostic on the account, with the benefit-limit report beside it.

vectors.name: 2001 403(b) is indeterminate because the IRC 403(b)(2) exclusion allowance still governs
vectors.description: Before EGTRRA, IRC 403(b)(2) capped the amount excludable from a tax-sheltered annuity at the exclusion allowance, and IRS Publication 571 (2001) chapter 5 computes the maximum amount contributable as the LEAST of that allowance, the IRC 415(c) limit on annual additions and the IRC 402(g) limit on elective deferrals. The allowance is 20 percent of includible compensation for the most recent year of service, multiplied by years of service, reduced by amounts previously excludable; that last term is a lifetime aggregate over the participant service with the employer and no ScenarioInput field supplies it. With the allowance unknown, the least of three cannot be identified, so no universal maximum exists and both the statutory maximum and the input-supported maximum are null rather than the 13500 the other two limits alone would produce (IRC 402(g) 10500 for 2001 plus the IRC 402(g)(7)(A)(i) 15-year catch-up of 3000). SOURCES.md already states this policy for legacy 403(b) exclusion allowances; before this vector the engines contradicted it. The IRC 415(c) pool is still reported without being consumed, and its limit is the lesser of the 35000 dollar amount and the 25 percent of 80000 compensation that IRC 415(c)(1)(B) then imposed, which is 20000. 2001 is the last governed year: EGTRRA (Pub. L. 107-16) section 632(a)(2)(B) struck IRC 403(b)(2), section 632(a)(3)(E) struck the IRC 415(c)(4) elections, and section 632(a)(4) applies both to years beginning after December 31, 2001.

vectors.name: 2002 403(b) is determinable because EGTRRA repealed the exclusion allowance
vectors.description: EGTRRA (Pub. L. 107-16) section 632(a)(2)(A) replaced the words "the exclusion allowance for such taxable year" in IRC 403(b)(1) with "the applicable limit under section 415", section 632(a)(2)(B) struck IRC 403(b)(2) outright, section 632(a)(3)(E) struck IRC 415(c)(4), and section 632(a)(4) applies all of them to years beginning after December 31, 2001. From 2002 the excludable amount is bounded by IRC 415 and IRC 402(g) alone, both of which this package encodes, so the account is answerable. Section 611(b)(1) raised the IRC 415(c)(1)(A) dollar amount from 30000 to 40000 and section 632(a)(1) replaced the 25 percent of compensation in IRC 415(c)(1)(B) with 100 percent, so on 80000 of compensation the annual-additions ceiling is 40000. Section 611(d) set the IRC 402(g) applicable dollar amount for taxable years beginning in 2002 at 11000, and IRC 402(g)(7)(A)(i) adds 3000 of 15-year catch-up for an employee with 20 years of service, whose 15000 lifetime cap and 5000-per-year service cap are both unreached, giving an employee-supported maximum of 14000. The remaining 26000 of annual-additions space needs an employer formula or after-tax permission, which is a plan term rather than a statutory unknown, so the status is determinate_with_assumptions and not indeterminate. This is the far side of the boundary the previous vector pins.

vectors.name: 1986 403(b) still reports the missing IRC 415(c) limit rather than the exclusion allowance
vectors.description: IRC 403(b)(2) governed 1986 as much as it governed 2001, but the package encodes no universal IRC 415(c) annual-additions limit before 1987, so the more fundamental gap is reported first and the account returns HISTORICAL_415C_LIMIT_INDETERMINATE with a null annual-additions pool limit. Both diagnoses reach the same answer of indeterminate and a null maximum, and stating the more specific missing figure is more useful than stating the exclusion allowance on top of it. This pins the ordering: the exclusion-allowance check sits after the IRC 415(c) check, so 1986 keeps the diagnostic it always had and the pre-2002 window observably begins at 1987.

vectors.name: 2001 401(k) is unaffected by the IRC 403(b)(2) exclusion allowance
vectors.description: The exclusion allowance was a term of IRC 403(b) and reached tax-sheltered annuities only; a qualified cash or deferred arrangement under IRC 401(k) was never subject to it. A 2001 401(k) on the same facts therefore stays answerable: IRC 415(c) is the lesser of the 35000 dollar amount and the 25 percent of 80000 compensation then required by IRC 415(c)(1)(B), which is 20000, and the IRC 402(g) limit for 2001 is 10500, with no age-50 catch-up because IRC 414(v) was added by EGTRRA section 631 only for years beginning after December 31, 2001 and the participant is 41 in any event. The 9500 balance of annual-additions space rests on an unknown employer formula. Pinning the control case is the point: the exclusion-allowance downgrade is scoped by account type, and a check written against the tax year alone would wrongly swallow every pre-2002 elective plan.

vectors.name: 2026 pension-linked emergency savings account is capped by IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i)
vectors.description: Notice 2025-67 states that 'The limitation under section 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) concerning pension-linked emergency savings accounts that may be included in certain types of defined contribution plans is increased from $2,500 to $2,600', so the 2026 figure is $2,600; the notice is committed under evidence/retirement-limits and fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt. IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions at the lesser of that figure and any lower amount the plan sponsor sets, so with $0 already attributable to the participant the whole $2,600 is available. It lands as a Roth deferral rather than a pre-tax one because IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account as a designated Roth account, and it consumes $2,600 of the $24,500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit the same notice states, because IRC 402A(e)(9) orders excess deferrals distributed under IRC 402(g)(2)(A) out of this account first, which only makes sense if its contributions count toward that limit.

vectors.name: 2025 pension-linked emergency savings room is the IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) cap less the participant contribution balance
vectors.description: Notice 2024-80 states that 'The limitation under section 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) concerning pension-linked emergency savings accounts that may be included in certain types of defined contribution plans remains $2,500', so the 2025 figure is $2,500. IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) forbids a contribution 'to the extent such contribution would cause the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions to exceed' that amount. It is a ceiling on a balance carried across years, not an annual allowance, so with $1,000 already attributable to participant contributions only 2500 - 1000 = $1,500 may still be accepted. Nothing in the year restarts the count.

vectors.name: a pension-linked emergency savings account already at the IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) cap accepts nothing
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) bars any contribution that 'would cause the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions to exceed' the limitation. A 2026 account whose participant-contribution balance already equals the $2,600 Notice 2025-67 states is therefore closed to further contributions: 2600 - 2600 = 0. The account is still determinate and still available — the answer is zero, not unknown — and no IRC 402(g) or IRC 415(c) capacity is consumed, leaving it for the participant's other accounts.

vectors.name: 2024 pension-linked emergency savings uses the unadjusted statutory IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) amount
vectors.description: Notice 2023-75 states no pension-linked emergency savings figure at all, and no earlier or later notice may be substituted. The amount comes from the Code: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) fixes the limitation at '$2,500', and the flush text of IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) directs the Secretary to adjust it only '[i]n the case of contributions made in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024'. 2024, the first year the account exists, is therefore governed by the unadjusted statutory amount rather than by an adjustment or by the $2,500 Notice 2024-80 separately states for 2025. The enacted text is committed as evidence/retirement-limits/sources/usc-26-402A.html and fixed by SHA256SUMS.txt.

vectors.name: 2023 has no pension-linked emergency savings account
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e) was added by section 127(e)(1) of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-328, div. T, title I), and section 127(g) applies the amendments made by that section to 'plan years beginning after December 31, 2023'. No such account could exist for 2023, so the account type is unavailable rather than merely uncapped, and the year carries no encoded limitation. Pinning the boundary is the point: 2024 is the first year, and neither the $2,500 the Code fixes for it nor any later adjusted figure may be reached back into 2023.

vectors.name: a pension-linked emergency savings account without a supplied participant contribution balance is indeterminate
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps 'the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions', a figure that spans every prior year and that IRC 402A(e)(7) — which requires the plan to allow withdrawal of the balance at least once per calendar month — can move downward mid-year. Nothing else in a scenario expresses it, and assuming an empty account would state a ceiling the statute may not allow, so the account is indeterminate with a null statutory maximum rather than defaulted to the full published figure. This mirrors the pre-2002 IRC 403(b)(2) treatment: a term the package cannot compute is declared, not omitted.

vectors.name: a pension-linked emergency savings account shares the IRC 402(g) limit with the plan's 401(k)
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account as a designated Roth account for purposes of the title, and IRC 402A(e)(9) provides that excess deferrals distributed under IRC 402(g)(2)(A) come first from the emergency account, which places its contributions inside the IRC 402(g)(1) limit rather than beside it. Notice 2025-67 sets that limit at $24,500 for 2026 and the IRC 415(c)(1)(A) annual-additions limit at $72,000. Taking the emergency account first by priority, it fills its own $2,600 IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) ceiling and the 401(k) then takes the remaining 24500 - 2600 = $21,900 of elective-deferral room. Both amounts are annual additions in the one IRC 415(c) group, which is far from binding at $72,000.

vectors.name: a plan sponsor's lower IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds below the statutory figure
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) sets the ceiling at the lesser of '$2,500' as adjusted — $2,600 for 2026 under Notice 2025-67 — and 'an amount determined by the plan sponsor'. A sponsor that sets $1,000 therefore caps this participant at $1,000, supplied as the plan-document employee deferral limit. The statutory maximum stays at the $2,600 the Code and the notice fix, because it reports the legal ceiling rather than the plan's; only the amount supportable on the supplied facts falls to $1,000. Keeping the two apart is the point: a lower plan term is not a lower law.

vectors.name: a pension-linked emergency savings account needs no birth year
vectors.description: Age matters to an elective-deferral account only through IRC 414(v), which lets a participant who attains age 50 exceed an applicable limit. No catch-up reaches this account: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) forbids any contribution that would push the participant-contribution balance past the ceiling, whatever the participant's age, and IRC 414(v)(3) does not displace that bar. A scenario supplying no birth year is therefore fully answerable — $2,600 for 2026 under Notice 2025-67 — and must not be downgraded by the missing-age diagnostic that a 401(k) or 403(b) in the same year would rightly raise.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's contradictory coverage tiers leave IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applicability unknown, self-only account listed first
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having family coverage for any month in which either of them has it, so an owner with a self-only month cannot be priced without knowing the other spouse's coverage: for 2026 the answer is either the undivided self-only 4400 plus the IRC 223(b)(3) age-55 1000, or a divided family limitation instead. Here the spouse owns two health savings accounts stating contradictory tiers, self-only and family. Coverage is one fact about a person, so the spouse has not stated whether they have family coverage, and whether IRC 223(b)(5)(A) reaches the taxpayer's self-only months is therefore unknown -- not merely the size of a shared limitation, but whether one exists. The taxpayer is indeterminate with a null statutory maximum and nothing allocated. This vector lists the spouse's self-only account first. Its companion lists the family one first and must produce identical output: the engine formerly kept whichever coverage statement appeared first in the accounts array and decided the applicability of IRC 223(b)(5)(A) from it, so these same facts returned a determinate 5400 in this ordering and indeterminate in the other. The two orderings differ in array position rather than in priority, because coverage facts are read in input order while priority governs allocation.

vectors.name: 2026 the same contradictory spouse coverage gives the same answer with the family account listed first
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having family coverage for any month in which either of them has it, so an owner with a self-only month cannot be priced without knowing the other spouse's coverage: for 2026 the answer is either the undivided self-only 4400 plus the IRC 223(b)(3) age-55 1000, or a divided family limitation instead. Here the spouse owns two health savings accounts stating contradictory tiers, self-only and family. Coverage is one fact about a person, so the spouse has not stated whether they have family coverage, and whether IRC 223(b)(5)(A) reaches the taxpayer's self-only months is therefore unknown -- not merely the size of a shared limitation, but whether one exists. The taxpayer is indeterminate with a null statutory maximum and nothing allocated. This vector lists the spouse's family account first; its companion lists the self-only one first. The pair exists to pin permutation invariance, which no single vector can state. The differing element is array position rather than priority: coverage facts are read in input order, so permuting priority alone would not distinguish the fixed engine from the broken one.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's coverage facts that conflict only in the annual deductible leave the other spouse determinate
vectors.description: The narrowing that keeps the two vectors above from overreaching. IRC 223(b)(5)(A) turns on whether a spouse has family coverage, and on nothing else. Here the spouse's two health savings accounts are still contradictory -- so the spouse is indeterminate under IRC 223(b) for their own accounts -- but both statements say self-only, so no reading of them puts family coverage on either spouse and the subsection cannot apply. The taxpayer's own limitation is therefore fully knowable: the 2026 self-only 4400 under IRC 223(b)(2)(A) plus the IRC 223(b)(3) additional 1000 for an account beneficiary who attains 55 before the close of the year (born 1970), giving 5400. The spouse's deductibles never enter it, because the lowest-deductible rule in IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applies only where the spouses have family coverage under different plans. Treating every conflict as unknown coverage would make this indeterminate, which would be a wrong answer to a question the record settles.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's coverage conflict outside the owner's eligible months leaves the owner determinate
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(1) sums twelve separate monthly limitations, and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats a spouse as having family coverage only for a month in which the other spouse has it, so the applicability of that subsection is a monthly question and not an annual one. The taxpayer here is an eligible individual in December alone, with self-only coverage, so IRC 223(b)(2)(A) gives one twelfth of the 2026 self-only annual amount of 4400, which is 366.67 to the cent. The spouse owns two health savings accounts whose statements contradict each other about January and say nothing about any other month; both therefore agree that the spouse has no family coverage in December, which is the only month that can affect the taxpayer. The spouse's own accounts stay indeterminate because coverage is one fact about a person, but the taxpayer's limitation is fully determined. Answering indeterminate here would suppress a December amount because of a January disagreement.

vectors.name: 2026 family sharing survives a spouse's conflict confined to an annual deductible that no longer applies
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives spouses who have family coverage a single family limitation, 8750 for 2026, and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides it equally between them absent an agreed division, giving the taxpayer 4375. Every operand of that calculation is agreed here. The spouse's two health savings accounts both state self-only coverage for the whole year and differ only in the plan's annual deductible. A deductible reaches the limitation in only two ways, and neither is present: IRC 223(b)(2) capped each month at one twelfth of the lesser of the deductible and the dollar amount only for 2004 through 2006, the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 having removed that cap for later years; and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) takes the lowest annual deductible only where the spouses each have family coverage under different plans, which a self-only plan is not. The spouse's own accounts remain indeterminate under the identical-person-facts contract, but an uncertainty that cannot reach an operand must not be projected onto the result that operand feeds.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's conflict between two family-plan annual deductibles does reach the shared family limit
vectors.description: The control in the other direction for the 2026 deductible vector above. For 2004 through 2006 IRC 223(b)(2) capped each month's limitation at one twelfth of the lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the statutory dollar amount, and IRC 223(b)(5)(A) takes the lowest annual deductible of the spouses' plans where each has family coverage under a different plan. Both spouses state family coverage here, so the deductible is an operand of the couple's single limitation, and the spouse's two accounts give different family-plan deductibles of 3000 and 4000. The lowest of the spouses' deductibles is therefore either 3000 or 4000 depending on which of the spouse's contradictory statements is true, and no reading of the record settles it. Every account sharing that limitation is indeterminate with a null IRC 223(b)(5) pool. A narrowing that let an annual-deductible disagreement through in this year would be a hole, not a refinement. The IRC 223(b)(5) shared limit is asserted null here as the control for the separation of the pool amount from its division: this disagreement is about an operand of the limitation itself, so it nulls the amount, and HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVISION_INDETERMINATE must be absent because the spouses never disagreed about the IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) shares. A split that let an amount disagreement report a number here would be the hole this control exists to catch.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's person-level family coverage contradicting their account's self-only leaves the other spouse indeterminate
vectors.description: The person-versus-account route to the same uncertainty, which involves no ordering at all. Coverage is one fact about a person, so persons[].hsaCoverage and that person's planRules.hsa are two statements of it and must agree; here the person-level statement says family and the account says self-only. IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having family coverage for any month in which either of them has it, so on one of those two statements the taxpayer's self-only months are recharacterized and on the other they are not. Whether the subsection applies is therefore unknown, and the taxpayer cannot be given the undivided 2026 self-only amount of 4400 as though the spouse had never said otherwise. Preferring the account statement over the person's, which is what reading a single retained statement does, would answer from the shape of the input rather than from the facts.

vectors.name: 2026 an HSA whose planRules.hsa states no coverage facts is a missing fact, not an assertion of no coverage
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) treats both spouses as having family coverage for any month in which either of them has it, so an owner with self-only months cannot be priced without the other spouse's coverage. The spouse here owns a health savings account whose planRules.hsa carries neither a coverage tier nor a monthlyCoverage list. That is a required fact left unsupplied -- the spouse's own account reports HSA_COVERAGE_FACTS_REQUIRED for it -- and not a statement that they held no high deductible health plan coverage. Reading the empty object as an assertion would hand the taxpayer the undivided 2026 self-only amount of 4400 on the strength of a fact nobody supplied, so the taxpayer is indeterminate and the diagnostic is the absent-facts one rather than the conflicting-facts one: nothing contradicts anything, something is missing.

vectors.name: 2026 an empty persons[].hsaCoverage is the documented statement of no coverage and leaves the other spouse determinate
vectors.description: The control for the vector above, and the reason the two empty objects cannot be normalized together. An empty persons[].hsaCoverage is the input's documented way to record that a spouse held no high deductible health plan coverage, which is an answer: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) can recharacterize a self-only month only where a spouse has family coverage in it, and this spouse has none in any month. The taxpayer's self-only coverage therefore stands undivided at the 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(A) self-only amount of 4400, with no IRC 223(b)(5) pool because the subsection never engages. Treating this statement as missing rather than as known absence would refuse an answer the caller did supply.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse's self-only-versus-no-coverage disagreement leaves the household ceiling indeterminate, all-year account first
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(5) household ceiling is the divided family limitation *plus* each spouse's undivided self-only months, so a disagreement that never touches family coverage can still change it. Both of this spouse's statements agree they have family coverage in no month, so whether IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applies to the taxpayer is settled; they disagree about whether the spouse held self-only coverage in January through November, and IRC 223(b)(1) sums twelve monthly limitations, so those eleven months are worth 11/12 of the 2026 self-only amount under one statement and nothing under the other. The ceiling the couple share is therefore not one number, and every account drawing on it is indeterminate with a null IRC 223(b)(5) pool. Answering from whichever statement the accounts array happened to carry first is what an ordering pair exists to catch. This vector lists the all-year statement first; its companion lists the December-only one first, and both must produce identical output.

vectors.name: 2026 the same self-only-versus-no-coverage disagreement gives the same answer with the December-only account first
vectors.description: The IRC 223(b)(5) household ceiling is the divided family limitation *plus* each spouse's undivided self-only months, so a disagreement that never touches family coverage can still change it. Both of this spouse's statements agree they have family coverage in no month, so whether IRC 223(b)(5)(A) applies to the taxpayer is settled; they disagree about whether the spouse held self-only coverage in January through November, and IRC 223(b)(1) sums twelve monthly limitations, so those eleven months are worth 11/12 of the 2026 self-only amount under one statement and nothing under the other. The ceiling the couple share is therefore not one number, and every account drawing on it is indeterminate with a null IRC 223(b)(5) pool. Answering from whichever statement the accounts array happened to carry first is what an ordering pair exists to catch. This vector lists the December-only statement first; its companion lists the all-year one first. The pair pins permutation invariance, which no single vector can state, and the differing element is array position rather than priority because coverage facts are read in input order.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's conflicting self-only deductibles reach the household ceiling in a capped year
vectors.description: The other half of the deductible narrowing. For 2004 through 2006 IRC 223(b)(2) capped each month's limitation at one twelfth of the lesser of the plan's annual deductible and the statutory dollar amount, and that cap applies to a self-only month as much as to a family one. The IRC 223(b)(5) household ceiling adds each spouse's undivided self-only months to the divided family limitation, so this spouse's self-only months are worth a different amount under a 2000 deductible than under a 3000 one and the ceiling is not one number. This is the case an earlier narrowing missed by requiring the conflicted person to have a family month: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) reaches the lowest deductible only where the spouses each have family coverage under different plans, which is why a self-only deductible never competes there -- but it is not the only way a deductible reaches the ceiling.

vectors.name: 2026 a person-level coverage statement does not disagree with the account that repeats it
vectors.description:
persons[].hsaCoverage states IRC 223(c)(2) coverage and nothing else. The owner-conflict detector compares every coverage statement made for one person, and the person-level statement is one of them, so a person who states family coverage and an account of theirs that states family coverage must read as one fact twice, not as two facts that disagree. Here the taxpayer states family coverage on the person and family coverage on their account, and HSA_CONFLICTING_COVERAGE_FACTS_FOR_OWNER must be absent.

Both spouses hold family coverage for all twelve months of 2026, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives the couple one limitation of 8750 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19 for the IRC 223(b)(2)(B) amount). The scenario states an agreed division of 1 to the taxpayer, which Notice 2004-50 Q&A-32 expressly permits -- spouses may divide "in any way they want, including allocating nothing to one spouse" -- so the taxpayer's account takes the whole 8750 and the spouse's account takes 0. Both are determinate: an agreed division is a settled one, and a share of 0 is a share, not a missing fact. Tax year 2026 is after the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 repeal of the IRC 223(b)(2) deductible comparison, so no annual deductible is an operand.

Before 0.5.0 this vector tested the same thing through the account-level familyLimitShare, whose structural absence from persons[].hsaCoverage had to be prevented from reading as a vote against an account that supplied one. That field no longer exists, so the hazard it guarded against is gone by construction; what survives is the coverage half of the comparison, which is what the vector now pins.

vectors.name: 2026 an age-50 catch-up fills pension-linked emergency savings room the 401(k) host's base pool has no space for
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) bars a contribution only "to the extent such contribution would cause the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions to exceed" the cap, so it gates a balance and is indifferent to how the contribution is characterised. IRC 414(v)(1) lets a participant who attains age 50 before the close of the year (IRC 414(v)(5)(A)) contribute in excess of an applicable limit, and 26 CFR 1.414(v)-1(b)(1)(i) enumerates the limits it relieves — IRC 401(a)(30), 402(h), 403(b), 408, 415(c) and 457(b)(2) — every one a plan- or employee-level limit and none of them account-level. The two compose, so a contribution the host's base limit can no longer accept may still be made within the account's own room. Here the 401(k) recognizes $24,500 of compensation and defers all of it, exhausting the $24,500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit Notice 2025-67 states for 2026 and leaving the emergency savings account no base capacity, while the host's own recognized compensation is spent so it takes no catch-up of its own. The participant attained age 56 in 2026, so the $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up the same notice states is still available, and the account's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) room of $2,600 less a $0 balance is filled from it: $2,600 is the lesser of the room and the $8,000 remaining. IRC 414(v)(3)(A)(i) provides that a catch-up contribution is not taken into account for IRC 415, so the annual-additions group is not charged for it, and the amount is Roth because IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account "for purposes of this title as a designated Roth account". The reported statutory maximum is the lesser of the host's statutory annual capacity ($24,500 + $8,000) and what the participant has contributed plus the room that remains ($0 + $2,600), so $2,600.

vectors.name: 2026 the same age-50 catch-up fills pension-linked emergency savings room on a 403(b) host
vectors.description: IRC 402A(f)(1)(B) names a plan under IRC 403(b) as an applicable retirement plan that may include a pension-linked emergency savings account, and IRC 402(g)(3)(C) makes an amount deferred under a IRC 403(b) annuity contract an elective deferral against the same IRC 402(g)(1) limit, so the host's base pool is exhausted exactly as the 401(k) case exhausts it. Nothing in IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) or IRC 414(v) turns on which of the two hosts the account sits in, so the same $2,600 of room is filled from the same $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) catch-up. This vector exists because the two hosts reach the allocation through different account types and traits, and a change that fixed only the 401(k) path would leave the 403(b) one reporting a maximum it never allocates.

vectors.name: 2026 a plan sponsor's lower IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds the base and the catch-up together

vectors.name: 2026 the pension-linked emergency savings balance and existing contributions are not subtracted twice
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) caps "the portion of the account balance attributable to participant contributions", a quantity stated as of the moment before the contribution in question. Room is $2,600 less $1,000 = $1,600, and that is what may still be contributed; subtracting the existing $600 a second time would charge the same dollars twice and would report $1,000. Reporting only the additional amount would leave the statutory maximum free to contradict the annual total, which is why all four figures are asserted.

vectors.name: 2026 a replenished pension-linked emergency savings account may take more in the year than the balance cap
vectors.description: IRC 402A(e)(7) requires the plan to permit withdrawal from the account at least once a month, and the Department of Labor's PLESA guidance states that a plan may not impose a separate annual contribution limit on the account, precisely because a participant must be able to replenish it after a withdrawal. Room is $2,600 less $200 = $2,400, the annual total reaches $600 + $2,400 = $3,000, and $3,000 exceeds the $2,600 cap without offending it, because at no point does the balance. A reading of the supplied figure as an opening or prior-year balance could not produce this result without a withdrawal input the package does not have, which is why the field is defined as the balance immediately before the proposed allocation.

vectors.name: 2026 a pension-linked emergency savings account needs a birth year only once a catch-up could reach its room
