Here the 401(k) has exhausted the $24,500 IRC 402(g)(1) limit, the account's $2,600 of room is untouched, and the participant still has compensation to defer, so whether a catch-up is available — a question only the birth year answers — decides whether the answer is $0 or $2,600. The engine reports BIRTH_YEAR_OR_DATE_REQUIRED_FOR_WORKPLACE_CATCH_UP and returns null rather than guessing, because an overstated ceiling is what exposes a taxpayer to the IRC 4973 excise. The owner's IRC 414(v) pool is deliberately not part of that test: it is sized from the very age in question, so it reads as empty exactly when the question is open.

vectors.name: 2026 a pension-linked emergency savings catch-up needs no prior-year FICA wages
vectors.description: IRC 414(v)(7)(A) requires that a catch-up contribution by a participant whose prior-year FICA wages from the sponsoring employer exceeded the indexed threshold be a designated Roth contribution, and this package asks for those wages so it can classify the catch-up. The test has nothing left to decide, and demanding a fact that cannot change the answer would make an age-50 participant's account indeterminate for no statutory reason. This vector is the same scenario as the 401(k)-host catch-up case with the prior-year wage figure removed; the amount, its Roth character and the determinate status are unchanged.

vectors.name: 2026 a 457(b) plan-document deferral limit lowers the contributable amount but not the statutory maximum
vectors.description: IRC 457(b)(2) permits a plan to provide that the amount deferred for a year not exceed the lesser of the applicable dollar amount under IRC 457(e)(15) and 100 percent of the participant's includible compensation. Both terms are encoded law applied to supplied facts, so both belong in the statutory ceiling this package reports: with $200,000 of includible compensation the binding term is the $24,500 IRC 457(e)(15) figure Notice 2025-67 states for 2026. A $10,000 limit written into the plan document is neither — it is a restriction the sponsor chose — so it lowers what may actually be deferred to $10,000 while the statutory maximum stays $24,500. That is the line README draws for `statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution` and the line the qualified-plan path has always drawn; the IRC 457 path previously folded the plan-document limit into the reported figure and returned $10,000.

vectors.name: 2026 a 457(b) account with no plan-document limit is unchanged by the statutory-maximum split
vectors.description: The control for the preceding vector. Splitting the IRC 457(b)(2) ceiling into the statutory figure — the lesser of the IRC 457(e)(15) dollar amount and 100 percent of includible compensation — and the figure the plan document further restricts must change nothing where the plan document supplies no restriction: both are $24,500 for a 2026 participant with $200,000 of includible compensation, so the deferral, the pool draw and the reported statutory maximum all stay where they were. Without this vector the split could silently move the ordinary case while the plan-document case alone was watched.

vectors.name: 2026 a sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount caps the balance and not the year's deferrals

Both clauses cap the same quantity -- a balance -- so the sponsor's amount is not a second, annual limit on deferrals, and the Department of Labor's PLESA guidance states that a plan may not impose a separate annual contribution limit on the account at all. $600 was contributed this year and withdrawn under the IRC 402A(e)(7) monthly withdrawal right, so the balance immediately before this allocation is $0 and the room is $1,000 - $0 = $1,000; the annual total reaches $600 + $1,000 = $1,600. Charging the year's $600 against the sponsor's $1,000 as well as against the balance would leave $400, stranding $600 of room the statute allows. The reported statutory maximum uses clause (i) only, because clause (ii) is a plan term: min($24,500 under IRC 402(g)(1) with no catch-up at age 36, $600 already contributed + ($2,600 - $0)) = $3,200.

vectors.name: 2026 an unwithdrawn balance leaves the sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) room correctly reduced
vectors.description: The control for the vector above, differing only in the supplied balance. Here the $600 contributed this year is still in the account, so the balance immediately before this allocation is $600 and IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) leaves $1,000 - $600 = $400 of room against the sponsor's clause (ii) amount. The annual total is $600 + $400 = $1,000, which is the sponsor's amount exactly, as it must be when nothing was withdrawn. Reading clause (ii) as a balance cap and reading it as an annual deferral limit give the same answer on these facts, which is why only the withdrawal case above distinguishes them; asserting both pins that the fix narrowed nothing. vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b)-hosted PLESA draws the IRC 457(e)(15) pool and not IRC 402(g)
vectors.description: IRC 402A(f)(1)(C) makes an eligible deferred compensation plan under IRC 457(b) of an IRC 457(e)(1)(A) employer a third applicable retirement plan that may hold a pension-linked emergency savings account. IRC 402(g)(3) enumerates elective deferrals exhaustively -- IRC 401(k) arrangements, IRC 402(h)(1)(B), IRC 403(b) salary-reduction annuities and IRC 408(p)(2)(A)(i) -- and no IRC 457(b) deferral is among them, so these contributions run against the IRC 457(e)(15) applicable dollar amount that IRC 457(b)(2)(A) imposes, $24,500 for 2026, and not against IRC 402(g)(1). IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(i) caps the participant-contribution portion of the balance at $2,600 for 2026, and the supplied balance is $0, so the room is the whole $2,600 and the base deferral takes all of it. IRC 457(b)(2)(B) caps the deferral at 100 percent of includible compensation, which at $200,000 does not bind.

vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b)-hosted PLESA joins no IRC 415(c) group even when one is supplied

An IRC 457(b) plan is in neither list, so no annual-additions limitation reaches this account whatever the caller supplies. Both accounts here declare annualAdditionsGroupId 'g', and the 401(k) alone uses it: it defers the full IRC 402(g)(1) $24,500 against a $72,000 IRC 415(c)(1)(A) limitation. The PLESA's second pool is its own IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) room rather than that group, which is the positive form of the negative claim -- an index that would hold a 415c entry instead holds the room.

vectors.name: 2026 the two PLESA hosts share no pool with each other
vectors.description: IRC 402A(f)(1) makes three plan types an applicable retirement plan, and a participant may hold an emergency savings account in more than one. So each takes its own $2,600 for 2026 and the participant contributes $5,200 across the two, which no single IRC 402A(e)(3)(A) balance cap could produce -- $5,200 is twice the 2026 figure. The $5,200 says nothing about the deferral limits, which are $24,500 apiece and could accommodate it either way; the pool identities asserted below are what separate those. The pool identities assert the separation directly: 402g:t against 457b:t, and one room pool per account.

The sibling account spends the IRC 457(e)(15) pool, and the participant has $20,000 of unused deferrals from prior years, so the extra available under IRC 457(b)(3) is min($24,500, $20,000) = $20,000, which exceeds the $8,000 IRC 414(v) catch-up. The statutory maximum is min($24,500 + $20,000, $0 + $2,600) = $2,600. The catch-up is Roth: IRC 457(b)(3) supplies the capacity, but IRC 402A(e)(1)(A)(i) treats the account as a designated Roth account for purposes of the title, so a participant contribution to it is Roth whatever limitation it was made under. vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) year needs no birth date, because IRC 414(v)(6)(C) removes the age catch-up
vectors.description: The same facts as the vector above but with no birth year supplied. It is made instead against the largest age-based catch-up 2026 could produce at any age: $11,250 under IRC 414(v)(2)(E) for ages 60 through 63, which exceeds the $8,000 IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) figure. The $20,000 available under IRC 457(b)(3) here is above that, so IRC 457(b)(3) is the higher limitation however old the participant turns out to be, the age is not load-bearing, and the result stays determinate at $2,600. The sibling account's own silence about the missing birth date is pre-existing behaviour this vector does not assert.

vectors.name: 2026 a governmental 457(b) PLESA needs a birth date once a catch-up could reach its room
vectors.description: The mirror of the vector above, without the IRC 457(b)(3) eligibility that displaced the age-based catch-up. Whether it can be reached turns on an age that was not supplied, so the account is indeterminate rather than reporting a confident zero. The question is asked only here: where the base allocation had already spent the room, or where IRC 414(v)(6)(C) had removed the catch-up, no age could change the answer and none is demanded.

vectors.name: 2026 a sponsor's IRC 402A(e)(3)(A)(ii) amount binds base and catch-up together on the 457(b) host

vectors.name: 2026 the sponsor's clause (ii) amount caps the balance on the 457(b) host too

vectors.name: 2026 an IRC 457(b)(3) extra below the year's largest age catch-up still needs the birth date

vectors.name: 2026 an inconsistent division leaves the division indeterminate but not the couple's limitation
vectors.description:
IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives spouses who each have family coverage a single family limitation, and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides that one limitation between them, "equally ... unless they agree on a different division". Those are two questions, and this vector holds the first answered while the second is not.

The amount. Both spouses state family coverage for all twelve months of 2026, so subparagraph (A) fixes the couple's single limitation at the 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(B) family amount of 8750 as adjusted by Rev. Proc. 2025-19. Tax year 2026 is after the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 repeal of the IRC 223(b)(2) deductible comparison, so no annual deductible is an operand and no coverage fact is in doubt. The IRC 223(b)(5) shared limit therefore reports 8750, as does sharedFamilyContributionLimit, whose contract is the limitation this owner divides taken before the share is applied. HSA_SHARED_FAMILY_LIMIT_INDETERMINATE must be absent: its text states that the limitation itself cannot be determined, which is false here. Collapsing the two flags back into one nulls the 8750 and fails this vector.

The division. hsaFamilyLimitDivision is stated as { status: "inconsistent" } -- the status for two records of one division that conflict. That is not the same input state as an agreed division, and it is not the same as silence either: silence would be statutory_equal and would divide 8750 equally, while "inconsistent" says the couple's own records do not establish what was agreed. Defaulting it to an equal split would assert an agreement the caller has just said cannot be made out, so no account's share can be stated: familyLimitShare is null on every account sharing the limitation, every statutory maximum is null -- a share of a known amount is unknown when the share is -- and HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVISION_INDETERMINATE is reported at ERROR for that reason. The amount is untouched, which is the whole point of the vector.

The taxpayer owns two health savings accounts, and they state identical coverage. That is what makes HSA_CONFLICTING_COVERAGE_FACTS_FOR_OWNER's absence load-bearing rather than incidental. Before 0.5.0 the division lived on the account as planRules.hsa.familyLimitShare, the owner-conflict detector compared whole planRules.hsa statements, and so a disagreement about nothing but the share was reported as a contradiction about coverage. Moving the division to the scenario is what removes that mislabelling: there is now no per-account field for the spouses' division to disagree in, so two accounts of one owner can differ about the division only by not differing at all. This vector fails if that field ever returns to the account.

vectors.name: 2026 an unknown division of a limitation of nothing is still determinate
vectors.description:

Both spouses hold family coverage for all twelve months of 2026, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives the couple the one IRC 223(b)(2)(B) family amount of 8750 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19). IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(i) then reduces that limitation by "the aggregate amount paid to Archer MSAs of such spouses for the taxable year", and the two spouses paid 5000 and 3750, aggregating to exactly 8750. 8750 - 8750 = 0, so there is nothing left for subparagraph (B)(ii) to divide.

The scenario states hsaFamilyLimitDivision as { status: "unknown" }, which ordinarily makes the division unstatable and nulls every account's maximum. It must not do so here. Every division of nothing is the same division: half of 0 is 0, an agreed 100/0 of 0 is 0 and 0, and so is every other split. The unknown cannot change any account's answer, so withholding an answer for it would report a limitation as unknowable that the statute has already fixed at a number both spouses can be told. Both accounts are therefore determinate at 0, HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVISION_INDETERMINATE is absent, and so is HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVIDED_EQUALLY_BY_DEFAULT -- there is no division worth announcing either.

Neither spouse attains 55 before the close of 2026, so no IRC 223(b)(3) additional contribution amount survives the reduction to keep a positive maximum alive; IRC 223(b)(5)(B) reduces the paragraph (1) limitation "without regard to" that amount, so a catch-up here would be reported beside the zero rather than inside it, and this vector deliberately excludes one so that the zero is the whole answer. HSA_ARCHER_MSA_CONTRIBUTIONS_REDUCE_LIMIT is reported because the reduction is what produced the zero.

vectors.name: 2005 an unknowable amount and an unknowable division are reported together and independently

vectors.name: 2005 an unstated spouse leaves a family-coverage owner's limitation indeterminate

vectors.description: The other half of the decision, and the reason widening the requirement costs a caller one field rather than an answer. That is an assertion, not a gap. With it the IRC 223(b)(5)(A) lowest-deductible comparison has exactly one candidate plan -- the owner's -- because a spouse with no coverage has no family plan to compete, so the couple's deductible is 5000 and the tax year 2005 limitation is one twelfth of the lesser of 5000 and the statutory family amount of 5250 (Rev. The "notwithstanding" is what decides it: subparagraph (A) deems both spouses to have family coverage, and that deeming does not make an ineligible spouse eligible for the division. So the taxpayer's share is 1 and the maximum is the whole 5000 -- not 2500, which is what an equal division between two eligible spouses would give, and not 5000 by way of an assumed agreement either. HSA_SOLE_ELIGIBLE_SPOUSE_TAKES_WHOLE_FAMILY_LIMIT reports the reason, and it is a different reason from HSA_SOLE_SPOUSE_ACCOUNT_TAKES_ONLY_ITS_EQUAL_SHARE, which is what a spouse who *is* eligible but owns no account produces.

vectors.name: 2026 an eligible spouse without an HSA halves the limit where an ineligible one would not

They are therefore an eligible individual under IRC 223(c)(1) -- owning an HSA is not a condition of that -- and IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides the couple's one limitation "equally between them" absent an agreement. vectors.name: 2007 an unstated spouse does not matter once the IRC 223(b)(2) deductible cap is repealed
vectors.description: The boundary that bounds the widened requirement. Section 303 of the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 struck the IRC 223(b)(2) comparison with the plan's annual deductible for taxable years beginning after 2006, so from 2007 the monthly limitation is one twelfth of the statutory amount alone. The lowest-deductible sentence of IRC 223(b)(5)(A) still exists, but with no deductible in the arithmetic there is no amount for a lower one to change: an unstated spouse's plan cannot move this figure. vectors.description: The check is not confined to the spouse route. IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) requires an annual deductible of at least 1000 for self-only coverage in 2005 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71); the owner states self-only coverage with a deductible of 800, so the assertion that this is a high deductible health plan's deductible is contradicted by the figure itself. Without the check IRC 223(b)(2)(A) would take the lesser of 800 and the 2005 self-only dollar amount of 2650 and report a confident ceiling of 800 derived from a plan that cannot qualify. The tier matters to the message but not to the outcome: each tier is tested against its own minimum. The three limitation fields in the published detail are withheld for the same reason the statutory maximum is: appliedAnnualLimitByMonth, proratedContributionLimit and contributionLimitWithoutLastMonthRule are all built from the rejected deductible, and a diagnostic that says the figure is not published as a ceiling cannot leave twelve copies of it one field away. The coverage months and the IRC 223(b)(3) amount beside them are not computed from the deductible and stay.

vectors.name: 2005 a self-only contradiction leaves the family limitation known and its division unknown
vectors.description: Notice 2004-50 Q&A-31 Example (1) with the self-only spouse owning an HSA of their own. Two questions come apart here and the engine must answer them differently. The *amount* is determinate: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) reaches the lowest annual deductible only among spouses who each have family coverage under different plans, so the spouse's self-only 200 plan is not a candidate however far below the 2005 self-only minimum of 1000 it falls, and the couple's single limitation is the lesser of the taxpayer's 5000 family deductible and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), which is 5000. The IRC 223(b)(5) pool therefore reports 5000. The *division* is not determinate. Q&A-31 divides only between spouses who are each an eligible individual -- “if only one spouse is an eligible individual, only that spouse may contribute to an HSA” -- and Example (1) gives H the whole 5000 because W's plan is not an HDHP. This engine does not test eligibility; it takes the caller's month list as the assertion of it, and here that assertion is contradicted by the same caller's deductible. So it cannot tell whether the 5000 belongs wholly to the taxpayer or is halved, and reporting 2500 would assert the very eligibility the deductible impeaches. Share null, maximum null, pool 5000. The engine must not also report HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVIDED_EQUALLY_BY_DEFAULT here: that is a statement that the division held at one half each, which is exactly the reading Q&A-31 puts in doubt, and it would contradict the null share reported beside it.

vectors.name: 2005 an agreed division of nothing to the impeached spouse is conclusive despite the doubt
vectors.description: The same Notice 2004-50 Q&A-31 Example (1) facts as the vector above -- the taxpayer holds a family plan with a 5000 annual deductible all year, the spouse holds a self-only plan whose 200 deductible is below the 2005 self-only minimum of 1000 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71) and so impeaches the eligibility their own month list asserts. The amount is unaffected for the same reason: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) draws only competing *family* plans into the lowest-deductible comparison, so the couple's one limitation is the lesser of 5000 and the 2005 family amount of 5250, which is 5000. What differs is that the spouses state an agreed division under IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) of 1 to the taxpayer, which Notice 2004-50 Q&A-32 permits -- "including allocating nothing to one spouse". That makes the doubt inconsequential rather than merely tolerable: on the reading where the spouse is ineligible, Q&A-31 gives the whole 5000 to the taxpayer and the spouse nothing; on the reading where the deductible is the erroneous fact, the agreement gives the whole 5000 to the taxpayer and the spouse nothing. Both readings produce the same two shares, so there is nothing left for the doubt to make unknowable and the division is stated: taxpayer share 1, spouse share 0. The taxpayer's maximum is therefore 5000 rather than null. The spouse's maximum stays null, and that is a different question with a different answer. Their share of the couple's limitation is settled at 0, but their own IRC 223(b)(1) limitation is not: their own stated deductible contradicts their own asserted eligibility, which leaves each of their monthly amounts untestable whatever the division says. So accounts.1.hsa.familyLimitShare is 0 while accounts.1.statutoryMaximumAnnualContribution is null -- a settled share of a limitation the owner may not be entitled to draw on at all. The absent HSA_FAMILY_LIMIT_DIVISION_INDETERMINATE is what this vector pins: the subminimum deductible is still diagnosed, because it is still contradictory input, but it no longer nulls a division that both of its readings agree on. The couple's total is 5000, the whole limitation, taken by the one spouse the agreement gave it to.

vectors.name: 2005 a deductible below the minimum by less than a cent is still below the minimum
vectors.description: The comparison is made at the cent precision every published figure carries, not with the tolerance this engine uses for accumulated floating-point error in its own arithmetic. A stated 999.991 is not a rounding artefact of any computation; it is what the caller supplied, and IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) requires at least 1000 for self-only coverage in 2005 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71). Subtracting a tolerance from the legal boundary instead would let this value through and publish a determinate ceiling of 999.99, visibly below the minimum the same engine encodes, so the consistency check must round the stated figure to cents and compare against the minimum itself.

vectors.name: 2005 two contradictory family deductibles are both diagnosed as coverage conflict and as subminimum
vectors.description: One owner's two HSAs state family deductibles of 1000 and 1500. Both are below the 2005 IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) family minimum of 2000 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71), and the two statements also disagree with each other, so two independent defects are present and both are reported: coverage is a fact about the person and must be identical on every one of that person's accounts, and neither stated figure can be a family high deductible health plan's deductible. The account is indeterminate on either ground alone. Which of the two figures the subminimum message names is fixed by taking the lowest, so that reordering the accounts cannot change it.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's subminimum family plan reaches only the months it was in force
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(A) resolves the lowest-deductible comparison month by month, so a contradiction confined to months this owner was not eligible cannot touch the months they were. The spouse holds family coverage in January only, with a 1500 deductible below the 2005 IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) family minimum of 2000 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71); the taxpayer holds family coverage in December only, with a lawful 5000 deductible. December has exactly one family plan in force, the taxpayer's, so its monthly limitation is one twelfth of the lesser of 5000 and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250, and the year is 5000 / 12 = 416.67. The spouse owns no health savings account, but IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) still divides the limitation equally between the spouses, so the taxpayer's share is half of it. Propagating the January contradiction across the year would refuse an answer the per-month comparison already has. No different division was agreed, so IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides that one limitation "equally between them" -- "them" being the married individuals of the opening clause of paragraph (5), not the spouses who happen to own an account. This account therefore takes half, and the other half belongs to a spouse who has no HSA to put it in and simply does not use it. HSA_SOLE_SPOUSE_ACCOUNT_TAKES_ONLY_ITS_EQUAL_SHARE reports that, and the status is determinate rather than determinate_with_assumptions because applying the statutory default is not an assumption. Reaching the whole limitation from this one account needs an agreement the spouses may make under Notice 2004-50 Q&A-32 and must then state as hsaFamilyLimitDivision { status: "agreed", taxpayerShare: 1 }.

vectors.name: 2005 the same subminimum family plan does reach a month the owner shares with it
vectors.description: The companion to the preceding vector, differing only in the month the spouse's plan was in force. Both spouses now hold family coverage in December, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) compares the two family plans for that month and the spouse's 1500 deductible is a candidate -- one that cannot be a family high deductible health plan under IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i), whose 2005 family minimum is 2000. The contradiction reaches this owner in the month they share, so the limitation is indeterminate. The pair pins that the scoping is by overlapping month and not by the presence of a contradiction anywhere in the year.

vectors.name: 2005 a spouse's January-only contradiction leaves the other eleven monthly limits reported
vectors.description: appliedAnnualLimitByMonth is month-granular by contract, and the IRC 223(b)(5)(A) lowest-deductible comparison it reports is answered per month, so a contradiction confined to one month must not erase the other eleven. The taxpayer holds family coverage all year with a lawful 5000 deductible; the spouse holds family coverage in January only, with a 1500 deductible below the 2005 IRC 223(c)(2)(A)(i) family minimum of 2000 (Rev. Proc. 2004-71). January is unknowable, so the annual figures -- the statutory maximum, proratedContributionLimit and contributionLimitWithoutLastMonthRule -- are null, because each is a sum over every month. February through December rest on nothing but the taxpayer's own lawful deductible and still report the lesser of 5000 and the 2005 family dollar amount of 5250, which is 5000.

vectors.name: an account-level familyLimitShare is rejected rather than read
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(5)(B)(ii) divides the one family limitation "equally between them unless they agree on a different division", and "them" is the married individuals of the opening clause -- the division is between spouses, not between accounts. The Instructions for Form 8889 direct the filer to "divide the amount on line 5 equally between you and your spouse" and to "complete a separate Form 8889 for each spouse"; Pub. 969 (2005) p. 5 adds that where a person has more than one HSA, "your total contributions to all the HSAs cannot be more than the limits discussed earlier". No authority divides anything between accounts. Before 0.5.0 the share was an account field, which let one owner's two HSAs state different divisions -- a state with no legal meaning that the engine then spent machinery detecting. The field is removed rather than normalised, because silently reading one of two contradictory account-level shares is how the wrong one gets used: an input that still supplies it is rejected with HSA_ACCOUNT_LEVEL_FAMILY_LIMIT_SHARE_REMOVED so the caller moves it to the scenario rather than discovering the change through a changed number.

vectors.name: an account-level IRC 223(b)(8) election is rejected rather than read
vectors.description: IRC 223(b)(8)(A) applies to "an individual who is an eligible individual during the last month of such taxable year", and IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(i) includes any resulting amount "in the gross income of the individual". Both operate on the person; neither speaks to an account. An owner with two HSAs therefore makes one election, and before 0.5.0 the engine carried a conflict detector -- computed identically, on the line adjacent to the one for the family-limit share -- whose only job was to notice two accounts of one owner disagreeing about it. The election now lives on persons[].hsaLastMonthRule and an account-level useLastMonthRule is rejected with HSA_ACCOUNT_LEVEL_LAST_MONTH_RULE_REMOVED, which is what makes the contradiction unrepresentable instead of merely detected.

vectors.name: an account-level testing-period fact is rejected under the same rule
vectors.description: The other IRC 223(b)(8) fields move for the same reason as the election itself. IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(iii) defines the testing period for "the individual", and IRC 223(b)(8)(B)(ii) excepts a failure "by reason of the death of the individual or the individual becoming disabled" -- the individual throughout, never the account. testingPeriodSatisfied on planRules.hsa is therefore rejected with HSA_ACCOUNT_LEVEL_LAST_MONTH_RULE_REMOVED and belongs on persons[].hsaLastMonthRule.

vectors.name: 2026 the spouses may agree to allocate the whole family limitation to one of them
vectors.description: Notice 2004-50 Q&A-32: spouses "can divide the annual HSA contribution in any way they want, including allocating nothing to one spouse". Rev. Proc. 2025-19 sets the 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(B) family amount at $8,750, and both spouses hold family coverage for all twelve months, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives the couple one $8,750 limitation. The scenario states an agreed division of 1 to the taxpayer, so the taxpayer's account takes the whole $8,750 and the spouse's takes nothing. Tax year 2026 is after the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 section 303 repeal of the IRC 223(b)(2) deductible comparison, so no annual deductible is an operand. This is the boundary Q&A-32 expressly permits, and it is expressible now as a single couple-level number where the account-level model needed two shares that had to be checked for summing to one.

vectors.name: 2026 a spouse allocated nothing of the family limitation keeps their own age 55 catch-up
vectors.description: Notice 2008-59 Q&A-22 asks whether each spouse must contribute their catch-up to their own HSA and answers "Yes. An individual who is eligible to make catch-up contributions may only make such contributions to his or her own HSA." IRC 223(b)(5)(B) divides the limitation determined "under paragraph (1) ... without regard to any additional contribution amount under paragraph (3)", so the IRC 223(b)(3) amount is not part of what is divided and an agreed division cannot reach it. Both spouses hold family coverage for all twelve months, so IRC 223(b)(5)(A) gives the couple the one 2026 IRC 223(b)(2)(B) family amount of $8,750 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19). The spouses agree under Notice 2004-50 Q&A-32 to allocate all of it to the taxpayer, which that Q&A expressly permits -- "including allocating nothing to one spouse". Both were born in 1968 and so attain 55 before the close of 2026, giving each the $1,000 IRC 223(b)(3)(B) amount. The taxpayer's account is therefore 8750 + 1000 = 9750 and the spouse's is 0 + 1000 = 1000, not 0: the agreed division exhausts the paragraph (5) limitation and leaves the paragraph (3) amount untouched in the hands of the spouse who earned it. The couple's total is 10750, the same as the equal-division case, because a division moves the family limitation between the spouses without changing it. This is the case the account-level model could not state, since a share of 0 on the spouse's account read as an incomplete division rather than as an agreed one.
